newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Nasdaq market makers settlement approved.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Nasdaq market makers settlement approved.

text.p: U.S. district Court Judge Robert Sweet Wednesday approved a settlement of a Justice Department antitrust suit against a group of securities firms who make markets in Nasdaq stocks.
Sweet approved a settlement that the securities firms and the government reached last July.

The settlement requires that securities firms tape record some conversations between brokers. Under terms of the settlement, the tapes cannot be used by private investors as evidence in any litigation they have against the firm.
Attorneys for the private investors in a separate class action suit opposed the settlement of the Justice Department suit because of the restrictions on use of the tapes.

"We are extremely gratified that the judge upheld the landmark settlement that continues to make markets more competitive," said Justice Department spokeswoman Gina Talamona. She said the settlement brings lower transaction costs to individual stockholders. As for the taping provision, she said "that will help us monitor the settlement."

The 24 Nasdaq market makers in the settlement include many of the biggest names on Wall Street including units of Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc., Morgan Stanley Group Inc., Goldman, Sachs & Co., CS First Boston; Lehman Bros Holdings Inc., PaineWebber Group Inc., Salomon Inc., Smith Barney Inc., Bear Stearns Cos. Inc., Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. and and the securities unit of J.P. Morgan & Co Inc.
Nasdaq was not a defendant in the Justice Department suit.

In its original complaint the Justice Department alleged that the market makers followed a "quoting convention" that was designed to deter price competition among the firms and other market makers in the trading of Nasdaq stocks.

The quoting convention resulted in the "spread" between a dealer's buying and selling price being artificially inflated. The department said that when certain buying and selling prices were changed in one-quarter point increments instead of one-eighth point, the effect was that the spread was never less than one-quarter.
